podcast.title: World Tour with Inspiral Carpets
podcast.body: For two years, Noel Gallagher toured the world with the Inspiral Carpets during what were described as some of the band's best years. "And for the next two years some of the best years of the Inspiral Carpets career. Noel toured the world with them looking after the guitars."

xref.title: Noel's Departure and End of Oasis (August 28, 2009)
xref.body: Immediately following the violent backstage incident in Paris, Noel Gallagher left the dressing room in a huff. Despite a tour manager announcing "five minutes to show time," Noel sat in a car backstage, then declared, "That's it. I can't do this anymore." Two hours later, a statement was posted on the Oasis website confirming his departure: "It's with some sadness and great relief to tell you that I quit Oasis tonight. People will write and say what they like, but I simply could not go on working with Liam a day longer." This marked the end of Oasis after 18 years. "Noel left the dressing room in a huff, just as someone declared that it was five minutes to show time. Noel sat in a car backstage for all of those five minutes, and when he came out, he said, that's it. I can't do this anymore."

xref.title: Noel's Detailed Account of Paris Brawl (2011)
xref.body: At a press conference two years after the Oasis breakup, Noel Gallagher recounted the Paris dressing room incident, describing Liam's behavior as "quite violent" and akin to "WWE wrestling" or "macho man Randy Savage." He detailed Liam's expletive-laden rant, the throwing of a plum, and Liam's return wielding a guitar like an axe, which nearly struck Noel's face before Noel destroyed it. This incident, witnessed by other band members who remained silent, was the final straw that led Noel to quit the band minutes before a scheduled performance. "Liam was quite violent. At that point, there hadn't been any physical violence, but it was a bit like WWE wrestling. And he was like the macho man Randy Savage. He was like, oh yeah, and all that going on. xref.title: Supernova Heights – £2.5M Gaudy Mansion, £700,000 Yellow Submarine Kitchen, Meg Matthews's Spending Habits
xref.body: At the peak of Britpop, Noel Gallagher and then-partner Meg Matthews bought a house at 8 Steeles Road in Belsize Park, London, for £2.5 million in the mid-1990s, naming it Supernova Heights in stained glass over the front door. The décor included zebra-print couches, wild animal prints, a gothic bed, handcuffs, and an estimated £700,000 spent covering the kitchen walls with tiny paintings of yellow submarines. Meg became nationally famous for spending approximately £27,000 per month on clothes and beauty products and £50,000 on a birthday party for their daughter Anaïs. During the divorce, Meg sought £40,000 per month; the settlement gave her a Regent's Park house Noel bought for £1.2 million, plus £25,000 per month in support. In summer 2007, Meg auctioned Supernova Heights furnishings on eBay, netting approximately $30,000 — illustrating how badly bad taste depreciates. Noel remains worth north of £50 million. xref.title: The Battle of Britpop with Blur
xref.body: Oasis and Blur emerged around the same time in the mid-1990s and quickly became intense rivals, fueled by class differences (working-class Northerners vs. comparatively posh Southern university lads) and perceptions of authenticity. In February 1995, after Blur won four Brit Awards, Damon Albarn of Blur attempted to congratulate Oasis at their number one party for "Some Might Say," but Liam Gallagher confronted him with bragging. Noel Gallagher also made highly offensive remarks about Damon Albarn. "One of the greatest and most intense was the fight between Oasis and Blur in the middle 1990s. This was definitely real and undeniably ugly."

xref.title: Valuable CD Singles with Bonus Tracks
xref.body: Oasis, particularly with Noel Gallagher's prolific songwriting, effectively utilized 5-inch CD singles by including three or four non-album tracks, such as studio recordings, demos, and live tracks, on each official release. These bonus tracks were highly collectible and some, like "Acquiesce," even became hits on their own. "No Galagher was cranking out so much music at the time that each official Oasis CD single came with 3 or 4 other non-album tracks, studio recordings, demos, live tracks. All the Oasis CD singles were worth collecting."
